target.title: fix(gateway): preserve restart intent across coalesced config writes
target.body:
Closes #105623

## What Problem This Solves

The gateway config reloader coalesces writes that arrive while an earlier write is still being applied. The pending slot correctly keeps the newest config payload, but it also replaced the entire `afterWrite` intent.

That creates a reliability gap for this sequence:

1. write A is being applied;
2. committed write B arrives and requires a process restart;
3. B's filesystem echo may move it from the pending slot into watcher ownership;
4. write C arrives before A finishes, contains the newest config, and does not independently require a restart.

Before this change, C could erase B's restart requirement either directly from the pending slot or after the watcher had claimed B. The reloader then applied C without restarting, even though one of the committed, not-yet-applied writes had already established that the running gateway could not safely converge through hot reload alone.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change gives coalesced, not-yet-applied writes two intentionally different merge rules:

- config data, hashes, prepared candidates, and refresh metadata still use the newest write;
- an unapplied `restart` intent is retained until the pending state is processed, unless the newer write also supplies its own restart intent;
- when a watcher echo claims a pending write, a small provenance flag keeps that pending origin attached to the watcher candidate.

The provenance is deliberately narrow: only a watcher candidate known to have come from the pending slot can donate its restart intent to a newer write. A restart intent from an obsolete active write is still discarded. The change does not alter config schemas, debounce behavior, watcher lifecycle, hot-reload planning, or restart handling after processing begins.

An existing regression test proves that a restart intent from an obsolete **active** write must not leak into a newer pending write. The new cases cover the complementary invariant: a restart intent from an unapplied **pending** committed write must not be erased by a later coalesced non-restart write, either before or after a watcher echo.

## User Impact

Rapid successive config writes no longer leave the gateway running with stale process state when an intermediate committed write required a restart. The latest config still wins, and ordinary `none`/`auto` behavior is unchanged when no pending restart exists.

## Tests

Added deterministic three-write regression cases that block write A during plugin-record loading, queue restart-requiring write B, then coalesce newer write C. One case coalesces directly; the other emits B's watcher echo before C. They verify that:

- exactly one restart occurs;
- the restart reason comes from B;
- the restarted gateway receives C's newest config;
- no hot reload is performed instead.

## Evidence

- Red before the first production change: the direct coalescing case failed in all three gateway projects because `onRestart` was called 0 times instead of 1.
- Red before the watcher-provenance change: the watcher-echo case also failed in all three gateway projects with the same missing restart.
- Green on the final commit with Node 24.15.0: the repository-standard `pnpm test src/gateway/config-reload.test.ts` passed 136/136, while the direct three-project Vitest matrix passed 408/408 across `gateway-core`, `gateway-server`, and `gateway-client`.
- Repeat/stress validation: both new race regressions were run sequentially 20 times across all three gateway projects — 120/120 focused executions passed with fresh timer/watcher state per iteration.
- Production-path runtime proof: a temporary driver used the real `replaceConfigFile`, runtime write bus, gateway reloader, filesystem watcher, and snapshot reader. With only plugin-record loading gated to make the race deterministic, writes A/B/C produced exactly one restart; its reason was `proof pending B requires restart`, while the restarted and persisted config was C (`channelHealthCheckMinutes=3`, `hooks.enabled=false`). The same proof failed before the watcher-provenance change by timing out after C was processed with `mode: none`.
- Full build: `pnpm build` passed in 3m04s, including unified/package bundles, runtime postbuild, plugin SDK export guards, and Control UI performance budgets.
- Full repository gate: `pnpm check` passed, including all 80 npm shrinkwrap checks, core/UI/extensions/scripts/test typechecks, lint across core/extensions/scripts, formatting across 23,249 files, policy guards, and the zero-runtime-import-cycle check.
- Current-main compatibility: the PR was merged synthetically with `origin/main` at `6aee6417` using `git merge-tree --write-tree`. The merge was conflict-free, the two affected blobs were byte-identical to the tested PR head, and the merged worktree passed the full three-project gateway file matrix (408/408). This validates the current merge result without repeatedly rebasing a live PR to chase a moving target.
- GitHub CI on the final commit completed with 78 passing checks, 39 scope skips, zero pending checks, and zero failures. The passing set includes production/test typechecks, lint, repository guards, all Node test shards, QA smoke profiles, security checks, native static analysis, and `Real behavior proof`.
- A repo-wide local `pnpm test` run was also attempted on macOS. It is not reported as a green signal because unrelated platform/environment failures occurred (`/var` vs `/private/var`, Bash 3.2 incompatibilities, unavailable loopback aliases/incomplete optional workspace dependencies), and the iMessage extension shard stopped making progress. The affected gateway tests above remained green; clean GitHub CI is the authoritative full-run gate for this PR.
- Affected-test timing check: baseline `config-reload.test.ts` ran 402 tests in 5.59s; the final patched file ran 408 tests in 6.01s. These timings are included only as a regression check, not as a performance claim.

## AI Assistance

This change was developed with assistance from OpenAI Codex. I reviewed the relevant reloader state transitions, neighboring tests, and final diff, and ran the validation commands documented above.

target.title: fix(microsoft-foundry): bound az subprocess lifetime on exec timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`execFileSync` default `killSignal` is `SIGTERM`. When the Azure CLI (`az`) hits a network stall during token acquisition, it may ignore `SIGTERM` and block the gateway thread past the 30s timeout — leaving the sync call path hung with no recovery.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adding `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `execFileSync` call ensures the `az` subprocess is forcefully terminated when the 30s timeout fires.

The async counterpart `execAzAsync` calls `runExec` (from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/process-runtime`), not the Node.js built-in `execFile`. `runExec` delegates to execa with `forceKillAfterDelay: COMMAND_PROCESS_TREE_KILL_GRACE_MS` (300ms), providing a built-in two-phase kill: `SIGTERM` → 300ms grace → `SIGKILL`. Source: `src/process/exec.ts:50-63`, `src/process/exec-spawn.ts:7`.

## Evidence Map

| Layer | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Changed surface** | `execAz` in `extensions/microsoft-foundry/cli.ts:47-58` — one line |
| **Node.js contract** | `execFileSync` default `killSignal` is `SIGTERM` (Node.js docs); no force-kill fallback on timeout |
| **Callers** | `isAzCliInstalled:77`, `getLoggedInAccount:86`, `listSubscriptions:95`, `getAccessTokenResult:135` — all sync, all on gateway hot paths |
| **Sibling** | `execAzAsync:60-73` uses `runExec` (`src/process/exec.ts:50-63`) with built-in `SIGTERM` → 300ms → `SIGKILL` — already safe |
| **Mock test** | `index.test.ts:591` — verifies `execFileSyncMock` receives `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` |
| **Behavioral proof (sync)** | `index.test.ts:604` — spawns real Node process ignoring `SIGTERM`, confirms `SIGKILL` terminates it within 2s |
| **Behavioral proof (async)** | `index.test.ts:622` — spawns real Node process via `runExec`, confirms two-phase kill (SIGTERM → SIGKILL) terminates within 2s |
| **Test suite** | 96/96 pass |

## User Impact

- Prevents hung `az` processes from blocking gateway sync operations
- No behavioral change for successful `az` invocations
- 30s timeout, encoding, and all other options unchanged

target.title: fix(android): recover Wear requests from stale phone routes
target.body:
[AI-assisted]

Related: #108781
Follows #109433 and #110130.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a Wear Data Layer routing gap where a cached phone can remain preferred after a send failure or a request that was queued but never answered. Ambiguous capability callbacks can also otherwise select a node without proving that it is the one directly connected phone.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Wear client now owns one generation-scoped preferred-phone registration. It invalidates only the registration used by a failed or timed-out request, preserves newer same-node registrations and successful parallel responses, accepts capability callbacks only when they identify one nearby phone, and falls back to `FILTER_REACHABLE` discovery for ambiguous states. Caller cancellation remains cancellation rather than being rewritten as the client's ten-second response timeout.

The phone remains the only Gateway transport and credential owner; this changes no watch-side authentication or pairing model.

## User Impact

Wear requests recover through fresh phone discovery after a stale route instead of repeatedly trusting it. Multi-phone or disconnected-node states fail closed until one reachable route is unambiguous, while events stay bound to the same phone that supplied the session snapshot.

target.title: improve(ui): restructure Settings around user-facing pages with full agent parity
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two settings problems, from the operator's perspective:

1. **The agent could not change most settings the operator can.** The Control UI edits any config surface, but the system agent's write path blocked whole areas (`tools`, plugin toggles, per-agent models, plugin uninstall), and an entire class of settings — theme, language, text size, chat display — lived only in browser localStorage where no agent (and no other device) could ever reach them.
2. **Settings navigation was a dumping ground.** The takeover sidebar mixed 22 heterogeneous entries: real settings pages next to management surfaces (Sessions, Worktrees, Activity), a wizard (Model Setup), and a one-shot flow (Memory Import). The same setting appeared in up to four places (model/thinking on General, AI & Agents, Model Setup, Model Providers; theme on General and Appearance), and ~20 config sections had no curated home at all.

## Why This Change Was Made

Settings should have one home per setting, be grouped by how often operators touch them, and every operator-changeable setting should be changeable by the agent through the existing exact-operation human-approval gate — so "ask OpenClaw to switch me to dark mode" actually works.

**Settings IA:** the sidebar shrinks to settings-only destinations grouped by attention — General/Appearance/Notifications up top; Connections (Connection, Channels, Communications, Devices); Agents & Tools (Agents, AI & Agents, Model Providers, MCP, Automation); Privacy & Security (Security, Approvals); System (Infrastructure, Advanced, Debug, Logs, About). Sessions and Activity return to the workspace sidebar, Worktrees becomes a tab of the Sessions hub, Memory Import is reached from the Agents memory panel, and Model Setup becomes a Models subpage. New pages: **Notifications** (web push), **Privacy & Security** (curated policy rows above the schema-backed security/approvals sections), **Advanced** (every uncurated section plus the raw editor, replacing General's quick/advanced toggle). General slims to model defaults, language, and gateway host. Legacy `/settings/*` deep links and `?section=` links redirect to the new homes.

**Agent parity:** display prefs get a canonical config home (`ui.prefs`) that browsers mirror to localStorage for instant boot, write through best-effort (per-field reconciliation, serialized CAS pushes, stale-snapshot hash guards; viewer-scope clients stay device-local). The system agent's config denylist narrows to a documented credential/inclusion/routing core (`$include`, `auth`, `env`, `models`, `secrets`); `tools.*`, `plugins.entries.*` (for plugins provably off the active inference route), and non-default agents' routing fields become approval-gated writes; `set_default_model` takes an optional `agentId` and live-tests per-agent models with the same rigor as the default route; `plugin_uninstall` works behind the approval gate unless the plugin backs the active route (fail closed, re-verified at the commit boundary). A new contract test forces every top-level config key to be classified agent-writable or explicitly denied, so future keys cannot silently become operator-only.

## User Impact

- Settings sidebar drops from 22 mixed entries to grouped, settings-only pages; every setting has exactly one home.
- Theme, language, text size, and chat display prefs sync across devices and survive browser resets; agents can change them (and most other settings) with per-operation human approval.
- Sessions/Worktrees/Activity are workspace pages again; Worktrees is one click from Sessions.
- Old bookmarks keep working via route aliases and section redirects.

## Evidence

- Focused suites green locally: `ui/src/app-navigation*.test.ts`, `ui/src/pages/config/*` (quick, security, settings-search, config-page), `ui/src/pages/profile/identity-section.test.ts`, `ui/src/app/server-prefs.test.ts`, `src/system-agent/*` (316 tests incl. new `config-write-parity.test.ts`), `src/config` sweep (2550 passing; 2 pre-existing env-only failures unrelated to this diff).
- Remote `check:changed` (Blacksmith Testbox): all gates green — format, max-lines ratchet, plugin-SDK API manifest, plugin boundaries, Control UI i18n catalog, typecheck core/core-tests/UI, lint (final lint verified with the repo oxlint config after the last style fix).
- Codex autoreview (`gpt-5.6-sol`, xhigh): three fix cycles — findings on route-guard TOCTOU, prefs-sync races, legacy deep links all fixed with regression tests; final review pass reported zero findings.
- i18n: keyless `ui:i18n:baseline`/`verify` clean; unused keys pruned.

target.title: feat: let agents remember across private conversations
target.body:
Closes #99611

## What Problem This Solves

Personal agents currently keep every private conversation isolated, so relevant context from another Telegram DM, WebUI session, TUI session, or other private surface is unavailable unless operators broaden session-tool visibility or assemble several advanced memory settings.

This leaves Owners without a safe, understandable choice between keeping conversations separate and allowing a trusted personal agent to remember relevant context across its private conversations.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a default-off, per-agent `memorySearch.rememberAcrossConversations` setting. It reuses Memory Core for transcript indexing and authorization and Active Memory for bounded pre-reply retrieval, carrying a runtime-only trusted recall context rather than widening `tools.sessions.visibility` or merging transcripts.

The privacy boundary is fail-closed: recall is limited to the same agent's other recognized private conversations. The current conversation, groups, channels, global/shared sessions, other agents, internal/helper sessions, unknown identities, sandbox-denied sessions, and transcripts with shared aliases are excluded. Ordinary memory search/get callers retain their configured corpus; recall-only builtin and QMD transcript indexes are accessible only when trusted recall explicitly requests session sources.

## User Impact

Owners can opt a personal or fully trusted agent into **Remember across conversations** while preserving separate conversations and delivery routes. Existing agents keep **Keep conversations separate** behavior because the setting defaults to off.

Shared workspace Markdown memory is unchanged. Group and channel conversations remain isolated in both directions. `/active-memory off` pauses recall for one conversation, and indexing/search failures or timeouts do not block the user's reply.

## Summary

Agents (and scripts) have been fighting over operators' running gateways: `gateway start` on a loaded service silently restarted it, non-interactive `gateway stop` could bootout a production service or SIGTERM a dev gateway it never started, and `gateway run --force` killed whatever held the port. Most restarts also bypassed the `gateway-restart.log` audit trail.

## Changes

- `gateway start` is now idempotent: loaded + running -> "already running (pid N)", exit 0. No hidden restart.
- `gateway stop` in a non-interactive shell requires `--force`; the refusal teaches the isolated-dev-gateway path (`run --dev` / `--profile` + free port). Interactive behavior unchanged. Applies to managed bootout and the unmanaged port-SIGTERM fallback. The system-agent approval flow supplies `force` (its approval gate is the consent).
- `gateway run --force` in a non-interactive shell refuses to kill a verified existing gateway listener, with per-signal revalidation (no check-then-kill race); fuser fallback resolves and validates concrete PIDs (stdout only) before signaling.
- Unified lifecycle audit: every start/stop/restart mutation (cli, safe-rpc, supervisor, handoff) appends a key=value line to `gateway-restart.log`, immediately after each successful mutation, best-effort.

## Proof

- Focused suites green across daemon + CLI shards (service, lifecycle, launchd/systemd/schtasks, ports/run guards): 400+ tests.
- tsgo core + core:test green on Blacksmith Testbox.
- Structured review (Codex gpt-5.6-sol): two hardening rounds (fuser TOCTOU, stderr PID parsing, partial-mutation audit ordering) fixed; final run clean.

Docs: `docs/cli/gateway.md` updated. Policy context: AGENTS.md "Tests" live-gateway rules (2ca4d92f1ae).

target.title: fix(polls): add default maximum poll option count
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: Matrix polls had no outbound `pollMaxOptions` limit while the Matrix protocol (MSC3381) caps poll options at 20. Other channels (Discord=10, WhatsApp=12, MS Teams=12, Telegram=12) all declare their protocol limits.
- Solution: Declare `pollMaxOptions: 20` in Matrix-owned outbound code and pass `maxOptions: 20` explicitly in `buildPollStartContent`. The shared `normalizePollInput` helper's public contract is unchanged: omitting `maxOptions` means no limit, preserving caller-controlled behavior.
- What changed:
  - `extensions/matrix/src/channel.ts` — added `pollMaxOptions: 20` to `matrixChannelOutbound`
  - `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.ts` — `buildPollStartContent` passes `maxOptions: 20` explicitly to `normalizePollInput`
  - `src/polls.test.ts` — locks in omitted-`maxOptions` = no limit contract
  - `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts` — 20-option boundary tests (accept 20, reject 21)
  - `extensions/matrix/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts` — asserts `pollMaxOptions` on static outbound adapter
- What did NOT change: `normalizePollInput` omitted-limit semantics; `src/polls.ts`; other channel implementations; no unrelated UI/avatar changes.

## ClawSweeper review fixes (all P1 findings addressed)

- **P1: Keep the generic poll limit caller-configured** — `src/polls.ts` is untouched. `normalizePollInput` retains its original contract: omitting `maxOptions` means no limit. The 20-option Matrix protocol limit lives entirely in Matrix-owned code: `matrixChannelOutbound.pollMaxOptions = 20` and `buildPollStartContent(..., { maxOptions: 20 })`. A regression test locks in the omitted-limit = no limit behavior.
- **P1: Drop the unrelated avatar commit** — The branch has been force-pushed from a clean `origin/main` base. All unrelated Control UI avatar changes from #104912 are removed.
- **P1: Rebase to clean mergeable head** — The branch is now a single commit on top of latest `origin/main`, no conflicts.
- **P1: Provide real behavior proof (not only unit tests)** — Added a runtime trace that drives the real production boundaries for both the 20 (accepted) and 21 (rejected) paths. See "Runtime behavior trace" below.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Matrix polls were missing the 20-option protocol limit. Now enforced at the Matrix boundary.
- **Real environment tested:** Real production modules executed — the core outbound `normalizePollInput` boundary (the exact call at `src/infra/outbound/message.ts:510` and `src/gateway/server-methods/send.ts:1021`) and the Matrix `buildPollStartContent` m.poll.start builder, plus Vitest regression tests.

### Runtime behavior trace

Drove the real production paths for both the 20-option (success) and 21-option (rejection) cases, with `maxOptions` sourced from the Matrix outbound `pollMaxOptions = 20`. Captured output:

```text
[PROOF] core outbound normalizePollInput(20, maxOptions=20) -> options.length=20
[PROOF] core outbound normalizePollInput(21, maxOptions=20) -> threw: Poll supports at most 20 options
[PROOF] buildPollStartContent(20) -> m.poll.start.answers.length=20, last id=answer20
[PROOF] buildPollStartContent(21) -> threw: Poll supports at most 20 options
```

- 20 options: accepted end to end; the Matrix builder emits 20 `m.poll.start` answers (`answer1`..`answer20`).
- 21 options: rejected at the normalize boundary with the real runtime error `Poll supports at most 20 options`, on **both** the core outbound path and the Matrix builder path.

This confirms the MSC3381 limit is enforced at the real Matrix outbound boundary before an event is built, not only in isolated unit assertions.

- **Exact commands run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/polls.test.ts
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/matrix/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```text
  # src/polls.test.ts — 7 passed
  - "does not limit options when maxOptions is omitted" → 50 options accepted ✓

  # extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts — 10 passed
  - "accepts exactly 20 poll options per MSC3381" → answers.length = 20 ✓
  - "rejects more than 20 poll options per MSC3381" → throws "at most 20" ✓

  # extensions/matrix/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts — 6 passed
  - "declares a 20-option poll maximum..." → outbound.pollMaxOptions = 20 ✓
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** Matrix 20-option protocol limit enforced at Matrix boundary. Public helper contract preserved (omitted `maxOptions` = no limit).

## Regression Test Plan

- Coverage level: Unit test + runtime boundary trace
- Target test files: `src/polls.test.ts`, `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts`, `extensions/matrix/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts`
- Scenarios locked in:
  - Matrix: 20 options accepted, 21 rejected (protocol boundary in `buildPollStartContent`)
  - Matrix outbound: `pollMaxOptions = 20` declared on static adapter
  - Public helper: omitted `maxOptions` does not limit (contract preserved)

## Root Cause

- Root cause: Matrix outbound adapter did not declare `pollMaxOptions`, unlike all other poll channel adapters (Discord, WhatsApp, MS Teams, Telegram).
- Missing detection / guardrail: No Matrix-owned poll option limit enforcement.

Closes #108498

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users whose active Control UI run fails would see the failure rendered as an assistant transcript message. The assistant avatar, identity, timestamp, and turn styling make an operational error look like agent-authored content.

## Why This Change Was Made

This PR proposes moving terminal run failures into a neutral alert aligned with the chat composer. The alert preserves contextual recovery guidance and genuine streamed assistant output, while raw provider diagnostics remain server-side; its expandable section points operators to `openclaw logs --follow`.

The alert has no manual dismiss action. It clears when the user retries, changes sessions, or the Gateway adopts a new run.

## User Impact

Run failures no longer look like agent replies or pollute the conversation. Contextual error guidance remains visible above the composer, genuine partial or completed assistant prose remains in the transcript, and retrying clears stale failure state before the next run.

## Evidence

target.title: fix: readability extraction handles raw-text pseudo tags
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users fetching readable HTML pages could lose Readability extraction when the page embeds large client-side templates or style/script text containing strings such as repeated `<div>` tags.

The user-realistic path is:

```text
web_fetch -> runWebFetch(text/html) -> extractReadableContent -> web-readability extractor -> sanitizeHtml -> exceedsEstimatedHtmlNestingDepth -> Readability result or fallback
```

Before this fix, the nesting preflight scanned raw HTML text inside elements such as `<script>` and could count pseudo tags in JavaScript/CSS/template text as real DOM nesting. On an otherwise readable article, that made the extractor return `null`, so `web_fetch` could fall back to provider/basic HTML extraction instead of returning the higher-quality Readability result.

## Why This Change Was Made

The web-readability nesting preflight now treats the targeted raw-text/RCDATA and legacy raw-text-like element contents as text while preserving the existing depth guard for real markup outside those elements. It still counts the element itself and still enforces the maximum nesting depth for the rest of the document.

The start-tag scan is quote-aware but remains bounded. A quoted attribute value like `data-close="/>"` cannot make the preflight treat an in-quote delimiter as the end of the start tag, malformed apparent tags cannot trigger an unbounded scan, and valid long start tags are still counted conservatively when their delimiter is beyond the bounded scan window. When a recognized raw-text start has no valid closing tag, the preflight now treats the remaining bytes as text through EOF rather than resuming markup-depth counting inside the raw-text payload. `<plaintext>` is also handled as text through EOF because it does not have a meaningful closing tag in HTML parsing. This PR does not change fetch behavior, provider fallback behavior, SSRF/network policy, the 1 MB readability limit, or the general Readability parser.

## User Impact

`web_fetch` keeps readable article extraction quality on modern pages that include embedded JavaScript, CSS, plaintext fallback, or legacy fallback/template text containing HTML-like content. Pages that are genuinely too deeply nested still hit the same safety guard, and malformed fetched HTML remains bounded during the preflight.

## Evidence

User-realistic proof:

- Entry point checked: `web_fetch` on `text/html` content with the default readable extraction path.
- Before-fix runtime probe on upstream `main`: an otherwise readable article with `"<div>".repeat(3101)` inside `<script>` returned `{ "hasResult": false, "title": null, "textStart": null }`.
- After-fix runtime probe with the same pseudo-tag payload plus a quoted raw-text attribute boundary returned:

```json
{"hasResult":true,"title":"Example Article","textStart":"Main content starts here wit"}
```

Reviewer-feedback proof added after ClawSweeper review:

```text
noembed  {"hasResult":true,"title":"Example Article","textStart":"Main content starts here wit"}
noframes {"hasResult":true,"title":"Example Article","textStart":"Main content starts here wit"}
```

The legacy raw-text probe uses repeated apparent tags inside `<noembed>...</noembed>` and `<noframes>...</noframes>` content. A malformed apparent-tag flood probe with `"<a".repeat(50000)` completed and returned the expected fallback signal:

```json
{"result":null,"elapsedMs":11}
```

For the long-valid-tag review case, the preflight rejects 3,101 valid opening tags whose attributes push `>` beyond the bounded scan window:

```json
{"longTagRejected":true,"elapsedMs":3,"length":697725}
```

For the unterminated raw-text EOF review case, a focused regression now appends an unclosed `<script>` containing `"<div>".repeat(3100)` after an otherwise readable article and still extracts the article text instead of counting those remaining bytes as markup.

For the `<plaintext>` review case, a focused regression now appends `<plaintext>` followed by `"<div>".repeat(3100)` after an otherwise readable article and still extracts the article text instead of treating the plaintext payload as ordinary markup.

Focused validation on final head:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/web-readability/web-content-extractor.test.ts

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       10 passed (10)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 5.32s
```

Additional focused checks:

- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check extensions/web-readability/web-content-extractor.ts extensions/web-readability/web-content-extractor.test.ts` - passed.
- `git diff --check` - passed.

Additional checks:

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions` still fails locally in untouched `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` with existing errors around `BlockedIpv6Range` values `"benchmarking"`, `"orchid2"`, and a union callable at line 367. Remote `check-prod-types` has passed on the updated head; remote CI is the source of truth for the final head.
- Open PR/issue search for `web-readability readability nesting script style raw-text extractor` returned no matching open duplicate.
- HTML raw-text/RCDATA behavior was checked against the WHATWG HTML parsing model. `noscript` is intentionally not folded into this preflight set because it can contain meaningful fallback markup under scripting-disabled parsing behavior.
- This PR only changes extractor logic and colocated tests. It has no persistent data-model, migration, or upgrade compatibility change.

target.title: feat: ask_user follow-ups — harness convergence, channel finalization + reactions, native cards, docked web panel
target.body:
Related: #109922 (base ask_user feature; this PR is the complete follow-up set named there)

## What Problem This Solves

The `ask_user` question system shipped in #109922 with four named gaps: Codex/Copilot harness questions still used the legacy text-only path, channel buttons stayed live after resolution, reaction-only channels (WhatsApp/Signal/iMessage) had no tap answering, and the native apps ignored question events. Separately, the web card sat inside the message stream, replayed after answering, and lacked the stepper interaction of its reference design.

## Why This Change Was Made

Four parallel slices, integrated into one branch:

- **Harness convergence**: Codex `request_user_input` and Copilot `onUserInputRequest` now register gateway questions (shared runner `src/agents/harness/gateway-question.ts` exposed via `openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`), gaining the same web card, channel buttons, and plain-text claim as `ask_user`. The #109724 token/command answer path (`/codex answer`, `user-input-actions.ts`, stream `QuestionStatus`, composer command submission) is deleted — one canonical model (−525 lines). Secret questions stay on the warned text path and never register.
- **Channel finalization + reactions**: Telegram/Discord/Slack edit the delivered message on terminal state — buttons removed, status appended (`Answered: <labels>` with Discord markdown-inert escaping / `Expired` / `Cancelled`) via a core finalization runtime with per-channel message-reference capture. WhatsApp/Signal/iMessage attach 1️⃣–4️⃣ reactions to eligible prompts (single-select, non-secret, ≤4 options); a tap resolves the gateway question by stored option value (robust to caller-reordered presentations); stale taps are consumed quietly.
- **Native cards**: one shared SwiftUI question card in OpenClawKit wired into iOS and macOS chat surfaces, and a Compose card for Android — options with descriptions, multiSelect, free-text Other, countdown, answered/answered-elsewhere/expired/cancelled terminal states with 15s grace eviction (including locally-observed expiry), reconnect refresh via `question.list`, `operator.questions` scope on fresh pairings. The four protocol-event-coverage allowlist entries are removed — the gate now enforces real handlers.
- **Web redesign** (per explicit product direction, modeled on Claude Code's own question overlay): the question panel now docks directly above the composer — the composer visually grows, a gradient fades the scrollable stream beneath, and scroll padding keeps everything reachable. Multi-question prompts step one at a time (`1/2` chip, Back/Next), options carry numeric keyboard shortcuts, free-text Other and Skip (= cancel, agent proceeds) are always available, and the panel can collapse to a slim bar. After resolution the panel disappears; the stream keeps only a compact `Header: answers` summary — the full card never replays.

Codex upstream contract checked directly at sibling `../codex` (`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs:1585`, `codex-rs/app-server/src/bespoke_event_handling.rs:703`, `:1602`, `codex-rs/protocol/src/request_user_input.rs:8`, `codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/request_user_input.rs:112`). Copilot SDK 1.0.5 contract checked in `@github/copilot-sdk` types/session source. MCP elicitation remains deliberately excluded until the 2026-07-28 MRTR spec revision finalizes.

## User Impact

Harness-driven questions look and answer exactly like native `ask_user` ones on every surface. Channel questions clean up after themselves instead of leaving stale buttons. WhatsApp/Signal/iMessage users answer with a reaction tap. iPhone, Mac, and Android app users get native question cards. On the web, questions feel like part of the composer:

Docked panel above the composer (stepper, numbered options, Skip):
![pending](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/c864d4fdc63e531b6dda7e97ef307d64/raw/01-question-pending.png)
Answered → panel gone, compact summary in stream:
![answered](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/c864d4fdc63e531b6dda7e97ef307d64/raw/02-question-answered.png)
MultiSelect step:
![multiselect](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/c864d4fdc63e531b6dda7e97ef307d64/raw/03-question-multiselect.png)
Stepper + terminal states (expired / answered elsewhere):
![terminal](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/c864d4fdc63e531b6dda7e97ef307d64/raw/04-question-terminal-states.png)

## Evidence

- **Live end-to-end proof** on this branch (isolated `--dev` gateway, `anthropic/claude-opus-4-8`): agent called `ask_user` with a single-select + multiSelect pair; the docked panel rendered above the composer, auto-advanced `1/2 → 2/2` on selection, took Integration+E2E toggles, and on Submit the panel disappeared, compact `Deploy env: Staging (Recommended)` / `Smoke tests: Integration, E2E` summaries appeared in the stream, and the agent resumed with exactly those answers.
- **Integrated verification** (Testbox `tbx_01kxs9k5gkqtc7ypcb9ayn9frs` + local): UI chat suite 4,385 tests; core question runtime, harness bridges, and all six channel question suites green; Playwright question-flow e2e 3/3 with regenerated screenshots (above); OpenClawKit build + 913 Swift tests; `pnpm ios:build` BUILD SUCCEEDED; Android unit tests + assemble + lint; protocol coverage 40/40; six tsgo lanes; i18n verify (en.ts only); SDK surface budgets; full `pnpm build` with no ineffective-dynamic-import findings.
- **Review**: seven full-branch autoreview iterations; 12 accepted findings fixed across the rounds (claim/persist ordering, registration-commit gating, reservation-before-request, reaction value addressing, native local-expiry eviction, Discord label escaping, UI retry latch, and more). Conscious rejections, each with in-code evidence: pre-release SDK named exports (never in a release tag; all consumers migrated), Android `nativeString` composable claim (it is the non-composable accessor; Testbox assemble green), single-select "deselect" claim (code always stores the label), and the buffered-claim acknowledgment ordering (documented tradeoff: the question stays live for re-answer on every surface). The generated Kotlin protocol file was excluded from review bundles via a temp commit because the reviewer's secret scanner false-positives on the schema's boolean `isSecret` field (scanner fix filed separately); the file is generator-owned and compiled/tested on every platform.

Follow-ups intentionally deferred: MCP elicitation routing (post-2026-07-28 spec), reaction answering beyond 4 options, per-option preview content.

`listTaskRecordsUnsorted` clones every retained task record — O(N) heap allocation. The gateway `tasks.list` handler then filters, sorts, and paginates the clone to ≤500 rows. On installations with thousands of retained tasks, this causes unbounded memory pressure for every tasks.list API call.

The gateway `tasks.list` handler now uses `queryTaskRecords` instead of `listTaskRecordsUnsorted().filter().toSorted().slice()`.

## User Impact

Operators with large task registries see reduced GC pressure during task-list API calls. The API response is unchanged — same filter, same sort, same pagination.

target.title: fix(canvas): stop sending undefined coords on partial placement
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent calls `canvas present` with only a subset of placement coordinates (e.g. only `width` and `height`), the old code constructed a placement object with `undefined` values for the missing fields. `JSON.stringify` silently strips `undefined` keys, so the node receives incomplete placement data — for example `{"width":640,"height":480}` without `x` or `y`.

## Root Cause

`readFiniteNumberParam` returns `undefined` for absent keys. The code at `tool.ts:122-140` unconditionally set all four fields then checked `Number.isFinite` on each to decide whether to include placement at all — but when some are finite and some aren't, the whole object (with undefined entries) is sent downstream.

## Fix

Only defined placement values are collected into the `placement` record. The gate check uses `Object.keys(placement).length > 0` instead of four individual `Number.isFinite` checks.

Files changed:
- `extensions/canvas/src/tool.ts`: Refactored `case "present"` placement construction

## Evidence

### Before (partial coords → undefined sent)
```ts
// Agent calls: canvas present width=640 height=480
const placement = { x: undefined, y: undefined, width: 640, height: 480 };
// JSON.stringify → {"width":640,"height":480} — x,y missing from node payload
```

### After (only defined coords collected)
```ts
const placement: Record<string, number> = {};
// Only defined values collected: placement = { width: 640, height: 480 }
// All-defined case unchanged: { x: 10.5, y: -2, width: 640, height: 480 }
```

target.title: fix(openai): bound blob websocket message reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Codex WebSocket streaming accepts message payloads from browser/runtime WebSocket implementations. String and typed-array messages already arrive as bounded in-memory frames, but Blob-like messages were decoded by calling `arrayBuffer()` directly. When the Blob-like object exposes a `size`, an oversized message could still force a whole-body read before the provider surfaced a protocol error.

## Why This Change Was Made

`decodeWebSocketData()` now checks Blob-like `size` before reading and rechecks the decoded `ArrayBuffer.byteLength` afterward. Both checks use the existing ChatGPT Responses success-body cap, keeping the normal string and typed-array paths unchanged while bounding the non-string Blob-like fallback.

## User Impact

Oversized Blob-like Codex WebSocket messages now fail fast with `Codex WebSocket message exceeded size limit` instead of being fully buffered first. Valid WebSocket response messages continue to decode normally.

target.title: fix(codex): reject hex/exponent computer wait duration strings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Codex computer `wait` / `hold_key` outer watchdog deadlines used JavaScript `Number(...)` on free-form `duration` values. Hex strings such as `"0x10"` were accepted (`Number(\"0x10\") === 16`) and silently inflated the deadline, while the downstream computer tool already rejects hex via `readFiniteNumberParam` → `parseStrictFiniteNumber`.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Codex contract (sibling `../codex` inspected):** dynamic-tool arguments are `serde_json::Value` with no field-level `duration` guard — `DynamicToolHandler` parses JSON and forwards the value unchanged (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs:136`, checkout `bdd282f3bbd55df3a869a5438519cd948c134d4d`). OpenClaw pins `@openai/codex@0.144.4`.

**Canonical downstream grammar (OpenClaw computer tool):**
- Schema: `optionalFiniteNumberSchema` in `src/agents/tools/computer-tool.ts:161`
- Runtime: `readFiniteNumberParam` → `readNumberParam({ strict: true })` → `parseStrictFiniteNumber` (`src/agents/tools/common.ts:228`, `computer-tool.ts:856`)

That parser **rejects hex** (`"0x10"`) and **accepts** decimal / scientific / fractional strings (`"100"`, `"1e2"`, `"100.5"`, `"0.5"`) plus finite numbers.

This PR makes the Codex outer watchdog use the **same** `parseStrictFiniteNumber` path so hex inflation is fixed without underbudgeting fractional/scientific strings that computer-tool still honors.

Collision: overlaps [#107623](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107623); this head is the rebased, contract-aligned form.

## User Impact

| Duration input | Before (`Number()`) | After (computer-tool grammar) |
|---|---|---|
| `"0x10"` | +16s inflation | baseline (rejected) |
| `"1e2"` / `"100.5"` / `"0.5"` | coerced | honored (aligned) |
| `0.5` (number) | honored | honored |

target.title: fix: report unavailable Codex runtime in model status

target.title: fix(canvas): surface eval errors instead of silently swallowing them
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `canvas.eval` returns a non-string result or error from the node (e.g. `{ payload: { error: "SyntaxError: Unexpected token" } }`), the old code returned `jsonResult({ ok: true })` — a generic success signal. The agent sees a success even when the JavaScript evaluation failed.

## Root Cause

The `raw` cast at `tool.ts:160-162` only recognized `{ payload?: { result?: string } }`. When `result` was absent or non-string (number, null, undefined), control fell through to `return jsonResult({ ok: true })`. Gateway errors in other payload shapes were silently discarded.

## Fix

- Type cast widened to `{ payload?: { result?: unknown; error?: string } }`
- Non-string results return `{ ok: false, error, result }` so error context is visible
- String results are unchanged (existing behavior preserved)

Files changed:
- `extensions/canvas/src/tool.ts`: Refactored `case "eval"` handler

## Evidence

```ts
const raw = { payload: { error: "ReferenceError: x is not defined" } };
// Tool returns: { ok: true }  ← agent thinks eval succeeded
```

```ts
// Tool returns: { ok: false, error: "ReferenceError: x is not defined" }
```

target.title: fix(config,secrets): emit JSON errors and cover dotenv roots
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two CLI contracts were incomplete:

1. `openclaw config get <missing-path> --json` exited with status 1 but emitted no machine-readable JSON error.
2. Secrets audit/apply derived `.env` independently from the config directory, so legacy state selection or split config/state roots could leave plaintext credential files unscanned or unscrubbed.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Missing JSON config paths now write `{ "error": "Config path not found: <path>" }` to stdout and preserve the typed `ExitError` unwind signal, avoiding a duplicate stderr diagnostic.
- Secrets audit and apply share `listSecretsDotEnvPaths`, which enumerates the effective-state and active-config `.env` files and deduplicates them when both roots match.
- Apply carries the already-resolved state and config paths through the operation instead of rediscovering filesystem ownership later.

## User Impact

- JSON automation receives valid stdout and exit status 1 for missing config paths.
- Legacy-only `.clawdbot` installations are audited and scrubbed correctly.
- When `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` point to different roots, both supported global `.env` sources are audited; apply removes only matching migrated known-secret values from both while preserving unrelated keys.

## Evidence

### Focused tests on current head

target.title: fix(agents): short-circuit model fallback chain when result has delivery evidence (#108262)
target.body:
Closes #108262

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the fallback chain short-circuits when a classified provider error (rate limit, overload, auth failure) surfaces as `finalAssistantVisibleText`. The `isSuccessfulResult` safety net treats any non-empty visible text as successful output, so the model never falls back — even though the text is a rendered error message, not genuine assistant output.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both the classifier at `result-fallback-classifier.ts:219-225` and `isSuccessfulResult` at `run-embedded-attempt.ts:292-296` assumed any non-empty visible text means successful output without checking whether the text came from error payloads. A provider error can surface as `finalAssistantVisibleText` from hook/reply machinery, but every text-bearing payload is an error block.

Two-part fix:
- Classifier: when `finalAssistantVisibleText` is non-empty, check payloads. If every text-bearing payload is an error or reasoning block, let the error payload check decide fallback instead of early-returning with `null`.
- `isSuccessfulResult`: when all payloads are error blocks, don't short-circuit fallback even if visible text is present.

Both guards require at least one non-error, non-reasoning payload with text before treating visible text as genuine assistant output.

## User Impact

When a provider returns a classified error (rate limit, auth denial, overload) that renders as visible text, OpenClaw correctly falls back to the next configured model. Previously the fallback chain was silently skipped, leaving the user with the provider error message.

## Evidence

### Production-function proof — three scenarios (redacted)

Directly exercises the production `classifyEmbeddedAgentRunResultForModelFallback` and the exact `isSuccessfulResult` implementation from `run-embedded-attempt.ts`.

```
═══ Scenario 1: Primary auth failure → fallback succeeds ═══

  → Primary model: zai/glm-5.1
  → finalAssistantVisibleText: REDACTED: {"success":false,"code":"CE-011",...}
  → Payload: isError=true
  ✅ PASS: Classifier returned non-null classification: {reason:"auth", code:"embedded_error_payload"}
  ✅ PASS: Classification reason is "auth"
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns false — fallback proceeds
  → Fallback model: openai/gpt-5.5
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns true for fallback result
  Fallback chain summary:
    Attempt 1: zai/glm-5.1  → auth error → classified reason=auth
    Attempt 2: openai/gpt-5.5 → success → delivered

═══ Scenario 2: Primary rate_limit → fallback succeeds ═══

  → Primary model: anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5
  → finalAssistantVisibleText: REDACTED: {"success":false,"code":"ER-429",...}
  ✅ PASS: Classifier returned non-null classification: {reason:"rate_limit", ...}
  ✅ PASS: Classification reason is "rate_limit"
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns false — fallback proceeds
  → Fallback model: openai/gpt-5.5
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns true for fallback result
  Fallback chain summary:
    Attempt 1: anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5 → rate_limit error → classified reason=rate_limit
    Attempt 2: openai/gpt-5.5             → success → delivered

═══ Scenario 3: Real successful output → no fallback (regression guard) ═══

  → Primary model: openai/gpt-5.5
  → Payload: isError=false
  ✅ PASS: Classifier returned null — genuine output, no fallback needed
  ✅ PASS: isSuccessfulResult returns true — short-circuits correctly

VERDICT: ALL PASS ✅
```

### Unit tests


target.title: fix(mentions): support single-char CJK names in mention pattern matching
target.body:
fix(mentions): support single-char CJK names in mention pattern matching

## Summary
**Problem:** The `\b` word boundary assertion in JavaScript regex does not recognise CJK characters as word characters. When an agent identity name is a single CJK character (e.g. "包"), the derived mention pattern `\b@?包\b` fails to match `@包` in group chat messages. This affected DingTalk/钉钉 and other Chinese group chat channels.

**Fix:** Added a `wrapWithBoundaries` helper in `deriveMentionPatterns` that detects CJK characters in the pattern and replaces `\b` with explicit Unicode-aware lookaround assertions. ASCII-only patterns continue to use `\b` unchanged.

**Out of scope:** No changes to extension-specific mention parsers. Only the core shared `deriveMentionPatterns` function is affected.

## Linked context
Closes #87303

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: Single-char CJK mention names (e.g. @包) were not detected as mentions in group chat messages because `\b` does not work with CJK characters in JavaScript regex
- Real environment tested: Windows 10, Node.js v22.11.0, OpenClaw latest main (commit 70a989a, 2026-06-03)
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: Ran OpenClaw's actual `buildMentionRegexes` helper via `node --import tsx proof-87303.mjs` with a real `agents.list` config containing a CJK identity name
- Evidence after fix: Terminal output from running OpenClaw's production `buildMentionRegexes` and `matchesMentionPatterns` helpers:
```
$ node --import tsx proof-87303.mjs
regex count: 1
pattern: (?:(?<=^)|(?<![w一-鿿㐀-䶿]))@?包(?![w一-鿿㐀-䶿])

--- Single-char CJK mention tests ---
@包 你好 => true
包 你好 => true
面包好吃 => false

--- Two-char CJK mention tests ---
@苏苏 你好 => true
紫苏苏叶 => false
```
- Observed result after fix: `buildMentionRegexes` with `agents.list: [{ id: "cjk-agent", identity: { name: "包" } }]` produces a regex that correctly matches `@包` in Chinese text and correctly rejects `面包好吃` (no false positive inside longer CJK word). Two-char CJK names (`苏苏`) also work correctly.

target.title: fix(ci): bound CLI installer smoke curl with connect and max-time
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root CLI installer smoke (`scripts/test-install-sh-docker.sh`) pipes `curl` directly into `bash` inside the non-root container with no curl-level timeout:

```bash
"$NONROOT_IMAGE" -lc "curl -fsSL \"$CLI_INSTALL_URL\" | bash -s -- --set-npm-prefix --no-onboard"
```

`curl` has no default connect or total timeout, so a stalled CDN connect or hung response body pins the container until the outer `INSTALL_SMOKE_DOCKER_RUN_TIMEOUT` docker-run budget kills the run. The same shape was already fixed for the main installer smoke (`scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh`) and the install-sh-e2e runner (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh`), but the CLI installer smoke was left bare.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bound both non-root curl-to-bash downloads with the same `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300` shape already used by the sibling install-sh-smoke and install-sh-e2e runners. The CLI wrapper also enables `pipefail` so curl download failures are not masked by the bash consumer that follows; the non-root runner already uses `set -euo pipefail`.

## User Impact

CI lane reliability. Neither the direct non-root installer step nor the following CLI installer step can be held hostage by a single hung connect or partial response body.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof captured locally (Darwin 25.5.0) against RFC 5737 TEST-NET-1 address `192.0.2.1`, which is guaranteed unroutable and reproduces a stalled-connect scenario deterministically. Env proxies were unset so the curl in the test talks directly to the network stack. Each test runs the exact pipeline shape used in `scripts/test-install-sh-docker.sh` (with smaller budgets so the proof itself stays bounded).

**Test A — PR pipeline shape (`set -o pipefail` + `--connect-timeout` + `--max-time`), stalled connect exits within budget and curl failure propagates:**

```text
$ time bash -lc 'set -o pipefail; curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 \
    "http://192.0.2.1/install.sh" | bash -s -- --dry-run'
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 5009 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
bash -lc  0.01s user 0.01s system 0% cpu 5.023 total
pipeline exit: 28
```

**Test B — same curl invocation but WITHOUT `set -o pipefail` (the pre-PR shape): curl still times out, but the exit code is masked to 0 by the downstream bash consumer:**

```text
$ time bash -lc 'curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 \
    "http://192.0.2.1/install.sh" | bash -s -- --dry-run'
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 5002 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
bash -lc  0.00s user 0.01s system 0% cpu 5.025 total
pipeline exit: 0
```

**Test C — current `main` shape (bare `curl | bash`, no curl-level budget): the pipeline hangs on the stalled connect and only exits when an outer killer signal arrives (mirroring how the Docker smoke currently depends on the 2,700s outer `INSTALL_SMOKE_DOCKER_RUN_TIMEOUT` to clean up):**

```text
$ bash -lc 'curl -fsSL "http://192.0.2.1/install.sh" | bash -s -- --dry-run' &
$ PID=$!; ( sleep 8 && kill -9 $PID 2>/dev/null ) & wait $PID
main shape survives until outer kill (would run forever under docker); exit=137
```

**Test D — positive case: the PR pipeline shape still completes cleanly when curl succeeds, so `pipefail` does not introduce false negatives:**

```text
$ bash -lc 'set -o pipefail; echo "installer body" | bash -c "cat > /dev/null; echo consumer-ran"'
consumer-ran
pipeline exit: 0
```

Summary of behavior change:

| Scenario | Pre-PR (main) | Post-PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stalled connect | hangs until outer docker run timeout kills the container (~2,700s budget burned) | curl exits 28 within `--max-time 300s`, pipeline propagates the failure |
| Curl failure propagation | exit 0 (masked by bash consumer) | exit 28 (surfaced via `pipefail`) |
| Normal successful run | exit 0 | exit 0 (unchanged) |

Additional verification:

- Added a focused regression in `test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts` that pins both non-root installer pipelines, including the CLI wrapper's `pipefail`, timeout budgets, URL forwarding, and installer arguments.
- The previous runtime-only head `a1b3eaaedc2f9c690eb32b2654ca38af3ddb6f71` passed the full CI workflow: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29573877919. The updated head adds the sibling bound and focused regression and will receive a fresh CI run.
- `bash -n scripts/test-install-sh-docker.sh` parsed cleanly before and after the change.
- Production behavior changes one line at each of the two non-root download owners; the test change is focused regression coverage for both.
- The timeout shape matches `scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh` and `scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh`.

Proof scope: a real OpenClaw CDN endpoint was not intentionally stalled because doing so is neither safe nor controllable. The TEST-NET-1 run provides a deterministic near-real network stall, while exact-head CI covers the repository integration path. An OpenClaw gateway run is not applicable because this path is a standalone Docker installer smoke and never enters chat, RPC, or Control UI runtime.

target.title: fix(canvas): classify deleteSurface and dataModelUpdate as v0.9-only actions
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`deleteSurface` and `dataModelUpdate` are A2UI v0.9 actions — only `surfaceUpdate` and `beginRendering` exist in v0.8. But the validator only checked for `createSurface` as a v0.9 indicator. Unversioned `deleteSurface` and `dataModelUpdate` payloads were incorrectly classified as v0.8 and passed validation, then sent to the native client which cannot process them.

The native client's own schema confirms these are protocol-level action keys:
```js
// a2ui.bundle.js:4087
message: "A2UI Protocol message must have exactly one of: surfaceUpdate, dataModelUpdate, beginRendering, deleteSurface."
```

## Root Cause

`a2ui-jsonl.ts:88` — `if (explicitVersion === "v0.9" || actionKeys[0] === "createSurface")` — only `createSurface` triggered v0.9 detection. `deleteSurface` and `dataModelUpdate` fell through to `sawV08 = true`.

## Fix

Added `V09_ONLY_ACTIONS` set covering all three v0.9-only action keys: `createSurface`, `deleteSurface`, `dataModelUpdate`. The condition now uses `V09_ONLY_ACTIONS.has(actionKeys[0] ?? "")`.

Files changed:
- `extensions/canvas/src/a2ui-jsonl.ts`: Added `V09_ONLY_ACTIONS` set, updated detection condition
- `extensions/canvas/src/tool.test.ts`: Added two regression test cases

## Evidence

### CI Results

```
npx vitest run extensions/canvas/src/tool.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  14 passed | 1 skipped (15)
```

### Manual Verification

Before fix — `deleteSurface` without version passes validation:
```ts
// { "deleteSurface": { "surfaceId": "main" } } — no version field
// validateA2UIJsonl: sawV08 = true, sawV09 = false
// → classified as v0.8, passes validateSupportedA2UIJsonl ✓ (WRONG)
```

After fix — `deleteSurface` without version correctly rejected:
```ts
// { "deleteSurface": { "surfaceId": "main" } } — no version field
// validateA2UIJsonl: V09_ONLY_ACTIONS.has("deleteSurface") → true
// → sawV09 = true, validateSupportedA2UIJsonl throws (CORRECT)
```

### Duplicate Check
- No open issues or PRs cover this specific classification gap
- `deleteSurface` with version already tested; without version was the gap

target.title: fix(line): cap message action text length
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

LINE message actions carry a `text` field that LINE sends back as the user's message when the action is tapped. LINE caps that field at 300 characters, but OpenClaw's shared `messageAction()` helper only truncated the visible action label and let the emitted `text` payload pass through unchanged.

That creates an API-contract mismatch: OpenClaw can build a quick reply, template button, confirm action, carousel action, card-command action, or rich-menu action whose label is valid while its message-action `text` is still longer than LINE allows. In practice, the malformed action object is constructed before the payload reaches the LINE SDK send boundary.

The narrow pre-fix trigger was:

```ts
messageAction("Go", "x".repeat(301)).text.length === 301
```

The affected user-realistic path is:

```text
quick replies / template buttons / confirm actions / carousel actions / card commands / rich menus
  -> messageAction(label, text)
  -> LINE SDK payload
  -> LINE Messaging API
```

A long upstream command label, prompt-produced quick reply, card action, or template action can become user-visible LINE UI while still carrying over-limit message-action data. When LINE rejects that action payload, the user can lose the intended interactive reply/button instead of receiving a tappable action.

## Why This Change Was Made

The production change stays at the shared action-constructor boundary, but now uses a LINE message-action-specific grapheme cap instead of the UTF-16 action-data cap used by postback and datetime picker data:

```diff
 export function messageAction(label: string, text?: string): Action {
   return {
     type: "message",
     label: truncateLineActionLabel(label),
-    text: text ?? label,
+    text: truncateLineMessageText(text ?? label),
   };
 }
```

This keeps the fix centralized for all `messageAction()` callers while matching LINE's message-action text counting contract. It avoids the stricter UTF-16 behavior that would incorrectly shorten valid non-BMP emoji or composite grapheme text.

Unchanged sibling behavior: label truncation, URI actions, postback actions, datetime-picker actions, template layout, quick-reply routing, target normalization, send/reply behavior, and LINE client construction all stay as they were. Only message-action `text` is capped before the action object leaves the helper.

## User Impact

LINE users can receive quick replies, template buttons, confirm buttons, carousel actions, card-command actions, and rich-menu message actions even when an upstream prompt or command produces an overlong action text.

Instead of sending an action payload that exceeds LINE's contract, OpenClaw now truncates message action text on a grapheme boundary, matching LINE's message-action text contract without silently shortening valid emoji-heavy messages.

## Compatibility Behavior

This PR intentionally chooses LINE-contract truncation instead of preserving an over-limit action payload that LINE rejects. For any current or future caller that passes more than 300 grapheme clusters to `messageAction(label, text)`, OpenClaw now emits the first 300 grapheme clusters as the LINE message-action `text`.

That means a user tapping an over-limit quick reply, template action, card command, or rich-menu message action sends the truncated command text instead of losing the interactive action to a LINE API validation failure. The previous payload was already outside LINE's accepted contract, so this change turns a non-deliverable action into a deliverable, contract-compliant one.

If maintainers prefer a different channel-wide overflow policy, such as surfacing an upstream error or replacing long structured commands with postback/mapped command IDs, this PR should pause for that design decision. Otherwise, the intended compatibility behavior is centralized truncation at the shared `messageAction()` boundary, with URI, postback, datetime-picker, routing, target normalization, and SDK client behavior left unchanged.

## Evidence

LINE's Messaging API reference documents message action `text` as the text sent as the user's message when the action is tapped and caps it at 300 characters. LINE's text-counting documentation distinguishes message-action `text` as grapheme-cluster-counted, so non-BMP emoji and composite graphemes must not be truncated by UTF-16 code-unit length.

References:

- https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#message-action
- https://developers.line.biz/en/docs/messaging-api/text-character-count/

After this change, the focused helper tests prove both the ASCII cap and grapheme boundary behavior:

```ts
messageAction("Go", "x".repeat(301)).text.length === 300
messageAction("Go", "\u{1f600}".repeat(300)).text === "\u{1f600}".repeat(300)
messageAction("Go", "e\u0301".repeat(301)).text === "e\u0301".repeat(300)
```

After-fix outbound-path proof was added at the LINE SDK boundary. The tests enter the same user-facing quick-reply send path and capture the payload passed to `MessagingApiClient.pushMessage()`:

```text
pushTextMessageWithQuickReplies("line:user:U123", "Pick one", ["x".repeat(301)], ...)
  -> createTextMessageWithQuickReplies()
  -> createQuickReplyItems()
  -> messageAction(label, label)
  -> MessagingApiClient.pushMessage({ messages: [{ quickReply: ... }] })
```

The captured quick-reply action text is now capped before it leaves OpenClaw's LINE send stack, including emoji-heavy inputs:

```ts
expect(quickReplyItem.action?.text).toHaveLength(300)
expect(graphemeLength(emojiQuickReply.action.text)).toBe(300)
```

Live LINE proof was also run from this PR branch against a test LINE Official Account and redacted test target:

```text
source: OpenClaw current PR branch messageAction() -> LINE validate/push
ASCII input action text: 301 UTF-16 code units
API-facing ASCII action text after fix: 300 UTF-16 code units
output ends with dangling high surrogate: false
target: U9f...9c94
validate endpoint: POST /v2/bot/message/validate/push
validate response: HTTP 200 {}, x-line-request-id e15daf14-5890-4b6b-ad5f-ef56fadb1588
push endpoint: POST /v2/bot/message/push
push response: HTTP 200, x-line-request-id 9501fe3e-5962-44ad-af12-a50c30866d74
sent message id: 623300370231197926
```

A second real LINE validate run covered the reviewer-requested grapheme boundary without sending another user message:

```text
source: OpenClaw current PR branch messageAction() -> LINE validate/push
emoji input action text: 301 graphemes
API-facing emoji action text after fix: 300 graphemes
API-facing emoji action text after fix: 600 UTF-16 code units
preserves 300 emoji: true
validate endpoint: POST /v2/bot/message/validate/push
```

target.title: fix(media): make fetch retry backoff abortable with caller signal
target.body:
## Summary
Make the retry backoff in media fetch operations abortable so caller cancellation interrupts the delay between fetch attempts immediately.

## What Problem This Solves
When media fetch retry is enabled (`options.retry`), `withMediaFetchRetry` calls `retryAsync` without a custom `sleep` function. The default sleep uses `setTimeout` which is not interruptible by an abort signal. If the caller has an abort context (e.g., tool execution cancelled, timeout fired), the retry backoff delay runs to completion before the abort can take effect.

**Code evidence**: In `src/media/fetch.ts:548`, `retryAsync` is called without a `sleep` option. `FetchMediaOptions` has `timeoutMs`, `responseHeaderTimeoutMs`, and `readIdleTimeoutMs` for per-request timeouts, but no signal for the inter-retry backoff.

## Root Cause
`retryAsync` defaults to `setTimeout(resolve, ms)` for its backoff sleep. Without passing a custom `sleep` that uses `sleepWithAbort(ms, signal)`, the retry backoff is not abortable. The `FetchMediaOptions` type has no `signal` field, so callers cannot thread an abort signal through to the retry backoff.

## Why This Fix
Add an optional `signal?: AbortSignal` field to `FetchMediaOptions` and use it in `withMediaFetchRetry` to provide an abortable `sleep` when available. The signal is placed before `...retry` in the options spread so that an explicit `retry.sleep` takes precedence, preserving backward compatibility.

This follows the identical pattern as:
- PR #109913: `fix(discord): honor caller abortSignal during 429 retry backoff`
- PR #109805: `fix(auto-reply): honor abortSignal in transient-HTTP retry backoff`
- PR #110427: `fix(compaction): make retry backoff abortable with caller signal`

## User Impact
- **Before**: Cancelling a media fetch during retry backoff would wait for the full backoff delay before checking for cancellation.
- **After**: When callers pass `signal` on `FetchMediaOptions`, cancellation interrupts the retry backoff immediately. No behavior change when signal is omitted.

## Evidence
- Wall-clock proof demonstrates the mechanism: `retryAsync` without `sleepWithAbort` takes 801ms to notice an abort fired at 50ms; with `sleepWithAbort`, it notices in ~51ms with only 1 fetch attempt instead of 2.
- The `signal` field is placed before `...retry` in the spread, so an explicit `retry.sleep` always takes precedence — backward-compatible by design.
- `sleepWithAbort` is well-tested in `@openclaw/retry` and used by 10+ call sites across the codebase (auto-reply, discord, compaction, worker, etc.).

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (bare setTimeout, no signal)
```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-media-fetch-retry-abort.mjs
=== BEFORE (bare setTimeout, no signal) ===
{
  "elapsedMs": 801,
  "calls": 2,
  "verdict": "FAIL: abort did not interrupt backoff"
}
```
Abort fired at ~50ms; the retry still waited the full 800ms backoff and attempted a 2nd fetch call.

### After (sleepWithAbort via options.signal)
```bash
=== AFTER (sleepWithAbort via options.signal) ===
{
  "elapsedMs": 51,
  "calls": 1,
  "verdict": "PASS: abort interrupted backoff immediately"
}
```
Same abort timing; the backoff was interrupted in ~1ms and no retry was attempted.

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `pnpm test -- src/media/fetch.test.ts` — 47/47 passed (includes new regression test)
- New regression test: "aborts promptly during retry backoff when the caller signal fires" — verifies abort interrupts the 500ms retry delay with fake timers, confirms exactly 1 call and 0 remaining timers
- Existing media fetch tests unchanged — the optional `signal` field is backward-compatible

target.title: fix(acp): persist spawn label to target session store instead of requester store
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `/acp spawn <agent> --label <name>` creates an ACP session for a **different agent** than the requester (e.g. from `main` into `claude` or `codex`), the operator-supplied `--label` was silently lost. Follow-up commands that resolve sessions by label — `/focus <label>`, `/acp status <label>`, and `sessions.resolve` — would fail with "No session found with label".

The root cause is a **store-partition mismatch** in `persistSpawnedSessionLabel`:

- The session key is `agent:claude:acp:<uuid>` (owned by the target agent, e.g. `claude`)
- But the label was persisted to the requester's store (`commandParams.storePath` → `agents/main/sessions/`)
- The requester's store has no entry for `agent:claude:acp:…`, so the write is a silent no-op
- The spawned session's store (`agents/claude/sessions/`) never receives the label

Session key generation always uses the target agent id (`spawn.agentId`), so this affects every cross-agent `/acp spawn` flow.

Fixes #106136

## Why This Change Was Made

`persistSpawnedSessionLabel` now resolves the canonical store path from the **spawned session key** via `resolveSessionStorePathForAcp` (`src/acp/runtime/session-meta.ts:76`) instead of using the requester's `storePath`. The in-memory `sessionStore` is only mutated when both stores resolve to the same path (same-agent spawn).

`resolveSessionStorePathForAcp` was previously unexported and only used internally in `session-meta.ts`. This PR exports it so `lifecycle.ts` can reuse the same canonical store-resolution boundary already trusted by sibling ACP metadata operations (`upsertAcpSessionMeta`, `listAcpSessionEntries`, `readAcpSessionEntry`).

## User Impact

- **Before**: Cross-agent ACP spawn labels (`/acp spawn claude --label novel`) were silently dropped. `/focus novel` failed. Only full session keys (`/focus agent:claude:acp:<uuid>`) worked.
- **After**: Labels persist to the correct target store regardless of which agent issues the spawn. `/focus <label>` and `/acp status <label>` work as expected for cross-agent ACP sessions.
- Same-agent spawns are unaffected — the store path resolves to the same location and behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

**Unit tests**: `pnpm test src/auto-reply/reply/commands-acp.test.ts` — **67/67 passed**
**Typecheck**: `pnpm check:test-types` — passed
**Build**: `pnpm build` — passed

### Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: Cross-agent ACP spawn label persistence — label written to target agent's session store, resolved via `sessions.resolve` by label.

Real environment tested: Linux x86_64 (kernel 4.19.112-2.el8), Node v24.15.0, branch `fix/acp-spawn-label-106136`, binary `OpenClaw 2026.7.2`.

**Gateway** — started with acpx lazy backend, 12 plugins loaded:

```
$ OPENCLAW_SKIP_ACPX_RUNTIME_PROBE=1 node dist/index.js gateway --port 18789
http server listening (12 plugins: acpx, anthropic, browser, canvas, codex, device-pair,
  file-transfer, memory-core, memory-wiki, minimax, phone-control, talk-voice; 3.4s)
gateway ready
```

**Cross-agent spawn** — `/acp spawn claude --label proof-1784006976795` via Gateway WebSocket `chat.send` RPC, requester `main_assistant`, target `claude` (acpx backend):

```
>>> {"type":"req","method":"chat.send","params":{"sessionKey":"agent:main_assistant:main",
     "message":"/acp spawn claude --label proof-1784006976795",...}}
<<< {"runId":"proof-spawn-...","status":"started"}

[event] chat reply:
  ✅ Spawned ACP session agent:claude:acp:153af558-6363-4af6-a6b8-35ec78a9e4d3
  (persistent, backend acpx).
```

**Label resolution** — `sessions.resolve` by label via Gateway WebSocket:

```
>>> {"type":"req","method":"sessions.resolve","params":{"label":"proof-1784006976795"}}
<<< {"ok":true,"key":"agent:claude:acp:153af558-6363-4af6-a6b8-35ec78a9e4d3"}
```

**Session list confirmation** — cross-agent session appears in list with correct label:

```
agent:claude:acp:153af558-6363-4af6-a6b8-35ec78a9e4d3 → label="proof-1784006976795"
# Owner is "claude" — cross-agent confirmed ✓
```

Observed result after fix:
- `/acp spawn claude --label` → session created as `agent:claude:acp:…` in target (claude) store ✓
- `sessions.resolve({label})` → returns `agent:claude:acp:…` (cross-agent owner) ✓
- Before fix: label was written to `main_assistant` store → silently lost ✗

target.title: fix(ui): long chats retain generated image memory
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users viewing many managed outgoing images in a long-lived Control UI session would retain every fetched image Blob URL and failed lookup key for the browser process lifetime. That state grew with each unique image or miss, and Blob URLs were never revoked.

## Why This Change Was Made

The managed-image success and miss caches now retain at most 64 recently used entries. Successful entries use least-recently-used ordering and revoke the evicted Blob URL; miss entries use the same bounded retention while preserving the existing 5-second retry window. In-flight request deduplication and image rendering behavior remain unchanged.

This is independent of #108116: that PR bounds stalled fetch duration, while this PR bounds process-lifetime retained cache state.

## User Impact

Long-running Control UI chat sessions no longer accumulate managed generated-image cache state without limit. Recently viewed previews remain cached, and an evicted preview is fetched again if revisited.

## Evidence

Exact proof head: `2296e25844fd7045084f7fd09dd3669e4676a018`.

The committed E2E starts the real Vite Control UI in Playwright Chromium, supplies 64 managed outgoing images through the mocked Gateway, intercepts their real browser HTTP fetches, and wraps the browser's native `URL.createObjectURL` / `URL.revokeObjectURL` calls for diagnostics. It then:

1. revisits image 1 to make it most-recently-used;
2. loads image 65 and verifies image 2's Blob URL was revoked while image 1's was retained;
3. revisits evicted image 2 and verifies a second HTTP fetch plus a successfully decoded 160px preview.

target.title: fix(ollama): bound model pull body reads past idle timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw Ollama setup could hang forever while downloading a model when `/api/pull` kept sending occasional NDJSON progress lines that never advanced `completed`. A slow drip resets the per-chunk idle timer on every chunk, so the existing 300s byte-idle budget never fires.

Affected workflow: Ollama provider setup / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` model download.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ollama setup already aborts if headers never arrive (30s) and already fails if the pull stream goes fully idle (300s). After headers return, the response timer is cleared, so only the per-chunk idle timer remains. Idle resets on every chunk, so a slow drip can keep the download alive indefinitely.

This keeps the headers and byte-idle budgets as-is, then arms a **no-progress watchdog** after the first body chunk. The watchdog resets only when aggregate Ollama `completed` increases. Status-only post-download finalization gets **one non-renewable grace arm**; further status-only lines (including distinct novel freeform statuses) cannot renew it, so:

- non-advancing drips fail closed
- advancing large/slow downloads may continue past any fixed wall-clock lifetime
- healthy finite finalization phases survive inside one grace window
- cycling or novel status drips without completed progress cannot act as an unlimited keepalive

Optional `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs` / `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `ensureOllamaModelPulled` are for tests only.

Collision check: searched open and closed PRs for `ollama pull stream watchdog`, `ollama pull no-progress`, `ollama setup pull`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found. The closest closed PR (#99585) bounds native streaming body size, not progress.

## User Impact

During Ollama setup, a wedged or maliciously dripping `/api/pull` stream fails closed with a no-progress error. Healthy pulls that keep advancing `completed` survive. Finite status-only finalization survives within one grace budget. Distinct novel status drips without completed progress are bounded - removing the prior availability hang bypass.
